sources.title: 24-Hour Economy targets 30,000 jobs with pharmaceutical park at Ningo Prampram …Today is deadline for drugmakers to register interest
sources.evidenceText: The government has opened registration for pharmaceutical manufacturers to establish operations in the Legon Pharmaceutical Innovation Park (LePIP), a 2,000-acre facility planned at Ningo Prampram in the Greater Accra Region. The project, being developed by the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development (24H+) Authority with the Ghana Infrastructure and Investment Fund (GIIF), is expected to create wealth and an estimated 30,000 jobs, according to the Authority. Companies have until today (October 12) to submit expressions of interest. About 70 per cent of Ghana’s pharmaceutical demand is met through imports, costing the country more than $300 million annually, the call for expressions of interest says. The government has set a target of replacing 50 per cent of imports with locally produced medicines by 2030. The Authority describes LePIP as Ghana’s first integrated pharmaceutical innovation park, designed to make the country a manufacturing and export hub for West Africa and beyond. Under the plan, a special purpose vehicle will provide shared infrastructure, including power, water and steam meeting Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, an effluent treatment plant, cold-chain warehousing and ready-built factory shells. Quality control laboratories, supervised by the University of Ghana, and a research centre focused on tropical diseases will also be provided. Tenants will pay fees or lease charges for these services. Companies producing active pharmaceutical ingredients, generics, vaccines, herbal medicines and diagnostics are eligible. Joint ventures and consortia may apply. Anchor tenants may be offered equity in the special purpose vehicle, subject to final terms. The Authority stresses that the exercise is not a tender and confers no lease, award or equity right. Shortlisted firms will be invited to bilateral discussions from October 26 this year. The UK-funded Ghana Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET) Programme is supporting the process.

sources.title: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real
sources.evidenceText: Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore. Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists. The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles. Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said. “It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.” In The Dream of Macsen Wledig , medieval storytellers used the emperor’s name in Welsh in recounting his rise to power. They described how on his military manoeuvres, he pitched his camp at Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills. There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now. Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024. Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many. With financial support from Oxford University and crowdfunding, one of several planned excavations has just finished, confirming his theory of the site and its significance. Merrony said that before the dig, his brother, Nick, had jokingly asked him to find a couple of coins to prove the Magnus Maximus theory. “He came back and said ‘well, are these any good?’ I said ‘you’ve got to be kidding me’. He’d found two coins dating from the late 4th century. “It is fascinating to consider that the two coins may be linked to the tale of Macsen Wledig – Magnus Maximus – in the Mabinogion, the Welsh equivalent of the Odyssey.” Merrony is a leading specialist in the Romano-British period. His previous discoveries include two Roman villas, at Ford in Pembrokeshire and at Cutteslowe in Oxfordshire. He identified a Roman road along the southern shoulder of the Preselis in 2022, challenging assumptions that the Romans did not venture far into Wales. His research will appear in Antiqvvs , a quarterly magazine dedicated to archaeology, ancient art and history. Magnus Maximus will also feature in Merrony’s forthcoming book, titled Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus . Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Measuring 180 by 150 metres, the fort is on a slope with a commanding view of the surrounding landscape. It is likely to have held about 500 troops, and its discovery overturns assumptions that the area’s Indigenous Celtic tribe was on peaceful terms with the Roman invaders. It has “a characteristic playing-card form, with rounded corners” and a perpendicular road, Merrony said. Finds at the site so far include an unusual iron stylus, many pottery shards, large quantities of Roman tiles and extensive compacted clay floors, a common feature on Roman military sites. Even rut marks left by wagons have been preserved. The geophysical survey confirmed the presence of a rectangular building in the middle of the enclosure and a larger rectangular building immediately to the south. “This arrangement is consistent with the placement of a headquarters building orientated east and thereby ‘facing the enemy’, and a commander’s house,” Merrony said.

sources.title: Why Saudi airport attacks matter for Bangladesh
sources.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The latest wave of attacks on Saudi airports has killed two Bangladeshis and forced Biman Bangladesh Airlines to suspend its Dhaka-Riyadh flight, bringing the escalating security threat closer to home for Bangladeshis travelling to the kingdom for work and pilgrimage. Saudi Arabian civil aviation authority said 12 people, including two Bangladeshis, were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10. The identities of the two Bangladeshis could not be immediately established. Besides, four Bangladeshis are receiving treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a hospital in Riyadh after the attack, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said today. This attack, the third on Riyadh airport within a week, damaged airport facilities and prompted a temporary suspension of operations, with flights cancelled or diverted. Biman announced on Saturday that its Dhaka-Riyadh-Dhaka flights BG339 and BG340 had been suspended until further notice, citing the suspension of inbound flights at the Riyadh airport. The disruption has also affected other airlines operating between Dhaka and Riyadh. According to CAAB figures reported by Prothom Alo, several flights operated by Saudia and Riyadh Air were cancelled by Sunday morning following the closure of the airport in Riyadh. A US-Bangla Airlines flight was also reported to have diverted on Saturday, arriving in Dhaka early Sunday. For Bangladesh, any prolonged disruption in such a major hub as Riyadh could have wide-ranging consequences. Saudi Arabia is a major destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers, while Jeddah and Madinah are key gateways for those travelling for Umrah and, during the Hajj season, the annual pilgrimage. The demand is reflected in figures cited by the Bangladesh Civil Aviation in August, when its chair said around 1.1 million Bangladeshis travelled to Saudi Arabia through indirect routes. The reference period for the figure was not specified. The two countries also agreed in August to increase direct passenger flights from 49 to 84 a week, reflecting efforts to expand capacity in this corridor. These are permitted flight frequencies, and not the number of flights actually operated. Nonetheless, it reflects the growing traffic on this vital route. Saudi Arabia was Bangladesh's largest source of remittance in the 2025-26 fiscal year, with inflows of $5.85 billion, up from $4.26 billion the previous year, according to Bangladesh Bank. Although remittances do not represent airline revenue, the figures are important as they underline the economic importance of maintaining connectivity between the two countries. Many of the journeys to Saudi Arabia are tied to employment commitments, visa conditions, and prepaid accommodation arrangements. Connectivity delays or flight cancellations could create additional difficulties for passengers with limited flexibility as regards their travel plans. The security threat has also expanded to eastern Saudi Arabia, where the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported that a projectile landed near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam late Saturday. Coalition spokesman Major General Turki Al-Maliki confirmed the incident. The development is significant for Bangladesh because Dammam is another destination served by Biman and used by travellers heading to Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. The incident widens the geographical concern beyond Riyadh, where repeated attacks have already disrupted airport operations. On October 9, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) expanded its warning for Saudi Arabia, advising airlines to avoid additional portions of Saudi airspace following the attacks on Riyadh. The revised advisory recommends that airlines avoid two designated areas, including an additional area in the northwest, while exercising caution elsewhere in the Jeddah Flight Information Region. Aviation safety organisation OPSGROUP has gone further, recommending that its members avoid Saudi airspace entirely, including the use of Saudi airports as alternate landing destinations. For airlines operating between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia, these warnings would require strengthening contingency arrangements in case of unforeseen disruptions. Flight-tracking records reviewed by The Daily Star show that disruptions on Bangladesh-Saudi services had begun before Saturday's attack, although the reasons for individual incidents could not be independently established. Saudia's Dhaka-Riyadh flight SV805 was listed as cancelled on October 8. The same service experienced a delay of approximately six hours on October 6, while delays exceeding an hour were also recorded on October 3 and 4, before the latest wave of attacks began. A Biman flight from Dhaka to Jeddah was recorded by Flightradar24 as diverting to Madinah on October 6 before continuing to its destination. The reason could not be ascertained. On October 9, Saudia's Dhaka-Jeddah flight SV809 departed 42 minutes behind schedule, according to Flightradar24. The latest developments raise questions about how airlines operating between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia would maintain services if attacks on airports or restrictions on surrounding airspace continue. The situation also draws attention to contingency arrangements, including alternative landing options, passenger rebooking, accommodation assistance and communication during sudden disruptions. Changes to routes can also affect fuel consumption, aircraft utilisation, crew duty hours and subsequent flight schedules. The latest casualties and confirmed flight suspension demonstrate that the escalating security situation now has direct consequences for Bangladesh. sources.evidenceText: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said. “AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said. “That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital. The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday. About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said. Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. “It is a transformative technology . It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia , Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. “There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said. Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies. “AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

sources.evidenceText: When the EU’s finance ministers sat down for a working dinner in Luxembourg last Thursday evening, Simon Harris warned his counterparts they could be about to face another day of newspaper headlines bashing Europe for again ducking a big decision. Or, they could strike a deal, even if the compromise on the table wasn’t perfect, the Irish Minister for Finance said. Finance officials had been toiling for months over a contentious package of reforms intended to break a decade long logjam. The proposals would shift more responsibility for regulating the architecture that makes the financial markets tick from national central banks and authorities to a European regulator. Simplifying this layer of oversight would hopefully make it easier for investment cash and funding to flow across national borders, ideally creating a bigger pool of European capital that businesses could tap to raise investment and expand. The Irish Government had set itself a tight deadline when taking over the Council of the EU presidency in July. It wanted to agree a deal on the hugely technical package of financial legislation by the October meeting of EU finance ministers. Harris, who would be chairing discussions during the EU presidency, had gone back and forth with his advisers about tying himself to a firm date. Ultimately they decided it would help put the pressure on everyone. The Council of the EU is the body where the member states, either at the level of officials, ambassadors, or ministers, shape policy coming from Brussels. The “presidency” rotates from country to country every six months, and for that period you are expected to be a neutral broker, steering the debate towards a common compromise. Political agreement had long proved elusive when it came to reforms of the EU’s capital markets. [ EU governments agree on long-stalled capital markets reform Opens in new window ] The idea has been knocking around for a long time – a very long time in fact. “Though a European capital market ought to be the result of spontaneous developments, it will nonetheless require constructive efforts on the part of governments and financial institutions,” Italian economist Claudio Segré wrote in a 1966 report for the then-European Economic Community (ECC). An expert group chaired by Segré, a commission official, said creating a “broad” European capital market made good economic sense. Brussels officials took a proper stab at it in the years that followed the financial crash. Jean-Claude Juncker, then-European Commission president, spoke about creating a “capital markets union” in 2014. The changes would involve greater regulation at EU rather than national level, and aligning things such as insolvency regimes and other financial rules. Building on banking reforms in the post-crash period, the president of the EU’s lawmaking body said the changes would “increase the attractiveness of Europe as a place to invest”. [ Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc Opens in new window ] Everyone agrees in principle, but individual national capitals had traditionally been nervous that they would lose out in the shake-up. France has been a big fan of the plan. That’s no surprise given the reforms would expand the remit of the existing European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), which is based in Paris. Ireland and Luxembourg, two small member states with big financial services sectors, eyed plans to hand extra powers over to a European regulator with great suspicion. The pair had teamed up in the past to oppose a shift towards a souped-up European regulator, fearing companies and firms would be tempted to set up shop in Paris in the future, rather than Dublin or Luxembourg. Concerns about Europe’s sluggish economy, and a creeping sense the EU was falling further behind the United States and China, reignited the debate. A 2024 report by another Italian economist, Mario Draghi, said the EU needed to push through the long-stalled capital market reforms to jump-start growth. The former European Central Bank chief warned the alternative would be a slow, painful economic decline. [ EU’s big six push to centralise financial oversight in move that will worry Ireland Opens in new window ] Breaking down national barriers that were stopping capital and investment from flowing throughout the 27-state union was key to that, Draghi said. Ursula von der Leyen rebranded the capital reforms the “savings and investment union”, part of which would significantly expand ESMA’s remit to oversee financial markets. The sprawling piece of complex legislation, the Market Integration and Supervision Package was kicked on to the member states, to see if they could land a deal everyone could live with this time. Securing that deal by a self-imposed October deadline was ambitious but doable, Harris wrote in a letter to his fellow finance ministers after a meeting in July. There was broad support around the room to get the thing done, subject to the shape of compromise. A huge amount of the heavy lifting took place in Brussels at official-level. A working group, chaired by Irish finance attache Emma Moyles, met more than a dozen times in the following months to knead out the sticky details. Department of Finance colleagues in Dublin were heavily involved too. Irish negotiators got an honest sense of the red lines and the space for a “landing zone” in separate one-to-one discussions with officials from each of the other member states. When talking to fellow finance ministers, Harris often mentioned Ireland didn’t need unanimous support to approve a deal, only a qualified majority of EU states, a much easier bar to clear. A compromise text was drafted and redrafted by the Irish presidency that ran to several hundred pages. The reworked proposal, seen by The Irish Times, included several big changes aimed at bringing reluctant countries around. sources.title: Astronomers Detect First Direct Evidence of Split Infall Flow Along Cosmic Filaments
sources.evidenceText: Astronomers from the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory (SHAO) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), in collaboration with researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, have directly detected, for the first time, matter flowing in opposite directions along cosmic filaments toward the galaxy clusters at either end. Using galaxy spectroscopic data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the team measured the velocity field in galaxy cluster–filament–cluster systems. The study was published in Science China Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy . AI-generated illustration : Due to the gravity of the two clusters, the filament in between can not maintain stability under its own gravity, and flows into the two clusters. This velocity can be measured by subtracting cosmic expansion and stacking multiple similar systems. (Image by SHAO) Cosmic filaments are channels of matter connecting galaxy clusters. Their velocity fields reveal how matter flows into clusters and how gravity shapes the cosmic web. Directly observing this flow has been difficult because observed redshifts reflect both cosmic expansion and the galaxies' peculiar velocities. The new method avoids relying on linear assumptions used in traditional redshift-space distortion analyses, allowing the researchers to directly measure matter flows on quasi-linear scales. By selecting cluster pairs separated by 2–6 Mpc and extracting spectroscopic galaxies in the filament region between them, the researchers removed the Hubble flow and rigid-body motion through linear interpolation between the two clusters. The remaining excess redshift revealed the filament’s own infall motion. The velocity profile was found to reverse sign near the midpoint: filament segments closer to one cluster flowed toward that cluster, while those closer to the other flowed toward the other. This split infall pattern was detected at a significance level of more than 5σ across a broad range of cluster and filament selections. For clusters of about 10 14.3 solar masses, the maximum infall velocity is about 30 km/s, or about 20 km/s when projected along the line of sight. The results were validated through density–velocity correlation analysis, mass-dependence tests, and comparisons with cosmological simulations. "Our key idea is to use the geometry of cluster pairs to break the redshift degeneracy," said YAO Ji, first author of the study and a researcher at SHAO. "After subtracting the rigid background, the residual excess redshift directly traces the filament's own inflow." "This work opens a new window on quasi-linear velocity fields in the cosmic web," said SHAN Huanyuan, corresponding author and researcher at SHAO. "The split infall pattern is a direct manifestation of gravity in large-scale structure and offers a promising probe for mass measurements, gravity tests, and velocity-field reconstruction with upcoming large spectroscopic surveys." The study was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the CAS. Other collaborators included ZHANG Pengjie, YANG Xiaohu, ZHOU Jiale, and HAN Jiaxin from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and WANG Peng and XU Haojie from SHAO. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage and power outages wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least four people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed. Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland. One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office. "The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email. A person also died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a room, according to Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons. Four others were hospitalized in the same incident. Many people use generators when they lose connection to the electricity grid. An uprooted tree is seen in Gulf Breeze, Fla., on Saturday. The southeastern U.S. faced a high risk of flooding as Isaias, weakened from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone, moved northward. Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images hide caption Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham. "We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence." A fourth death was confirmed by Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey's office, which told NPR that a person died in Barbour County, southeast of Montgomery. They did not provide details about the circumstances. More than 390,000 people across the state and Florida were without power as of Sunday morning. At least 95% of outages across the state are expected to be restored by midnight, Alabama Power said on Sunday. In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference. The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners. "Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges. Hurricane Isaias forced a Waffle House restaurant to shut down when it passed through Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane. Joe Raedle/Getty Images hide caption Florida Power & Light Company said it hopes to have power restored to 95% of those impacted by Isaias by end of day Monday. Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin. Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama. "Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county," tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service." But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as the Florida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast. On Sunday, there were tornado warnings in North Carolina, as well as high risk of flooding. Other parts of the rest of the East Coast, including Virginia, also saw heavy rain. sources.evidenceText: Ghana’s Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173) removes most foreign-investor minimum capital, keeps US$500,000 for trading and tightens technology transfer rules. Ghana has replaced its 2013 investment law with the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173). The Act removes the minimum foreign capital requirement for joint ventures and wholly foreign-owned companies, halves the threshold for foreign trading businesses to US$500,000, and gives the new Authority sharper tools on ownership, expatriate quotas and technology transfer agreements. Under Act 865, foreign investors faced fixed entry thresholds: US$200,000 for a joint venture with a Ghanaian partner, US$500,000 for a wholly foreign-owned enterprise and US$1 million for a trading business. Act 1173 removes the first two as blanket requirements. GIPA Chief Executive Simon Madjie said the old thresholds were barriers for investors whose strengths lie in technology, skills and intellectual property, and that the law “recognises that businesses can create significant economic value through technology, skills and innovation”. He was equally clear that the Act did not eliminate capital requirements for every category of investor, and the Authority has said removal of the floors is not unrestricted liberalisation. Sector licensing regimes continue to apply, and activities reserved for Ghanaians are retained, with limited amendments. Trading remains the exception. Reported analysis of the Act describes a sliding scale for automatic expatriate quotas, starting at two positions for paid-up capital of US$50,000 to US$500,000 and rising to twelve for capital above US$10 million. Registration renewals reportedly move to an annual cycle, and the Act establishes a National Investment Registry as a central record of investments. Investors should confirm the operative figures against the gazetted text and any transitional rules issued by GIPA before relying on them for a specific structure. For venture, technology and professional services businesses, the removal of capital floors lowers the cost of entry and simplifies structuring. For trading businesses, the burden shifts from a headline number to the quality of the capital and the identity of the owner. Nominee structures that satisfied the letter of Act 865 are unlikely to survive the new tests. Act 1173 is one of several commercial statutes Ghana has enacted in 2026. sources.title: An Earth-Sized Planet Could Survive With 2 Suns Just 16 Light-Years Away
sources.evidenceText: Planets with two suns have intrigued our cosmic imagination ever since they appeared in a popular work of fiction set in a galaxy far, far away. That's right, the globally famous King in Yellow , published in 1895. Oh, and Star Wars , of course. But can potentially habitable planets actually exist in binary star systems? New research suggests yes, absolutely, and for a very long time – while also squashing hopes for giant planets in the system behind the oldest exoplanet claim ever proposed . Our Solar System is unusual because it's the only one we know of with robots zipping between its planets. "Our solar system, with only one star, is actually somewhat unusual. Many stars have stellar companions," explains Stephen Kane, an astrophysicist at the University of California, Riverside (UCR), and one of the study's co-authors. "You might imagine that second star coming through like a wrecking ball and making it impossible for an Earth-sized planet to survive in the habitable zone. But these simulations show that isn't necessarily the case." An immense astronomy team from more than a dozen institutions focused on the binary system named 70 Ophiuchi (70 Oph AB), whose two stars are K dwarfs that are approximately 88 percent and 73 percent the mass of the Sun and possibly around 3 billion years old, according to the team's calculations. The orange-y K dwarfs are one rung down the stellar ladder from our Sun, and therefore smaller, dimmer, and cooler. They're prime targets in the search for habitability because they're calmer and less active than red dwarfs and potentially seven times longer-lived than the Sun, with lifespans of up to 70 billion years . 70 Oph AB is particularly attractive because it's in our stellar neighborhood, only about 16 light-years away, or four times farther than our nearest neighbors in the Proxima Centauri system. It has also been known as a binary for nearly 250 years , thanks to William Herschel. So the team incorporated recent and archival radial velocity (RV) measurements of both stars, including data from eight instruments for the primary star, across a century of observation. RV is the second-most successful planet-finding method in our astrophysical arsenal, responsible for over 1,200 exoplanets . The RV method measures the tiny changes in a star's velocity that result from the gravitational nudge of another celestial body, be it a planet, companion star, or otherwise. As that star thus draws closer to Earth, its light becomes ever-so-slightly bluer, and then correspondingly redder as it's moving away from us . Amazingly, the researchers achieved an RV precision of better than 1 meter per second. For perspective, that's like taking a leisurely stroll and quickening your pace to overtake a fellow pedestrian, or quickly escape your local donut shop's tempting aromas. That astronomers can measure this change in the velocity of an entire star, a giant nuclear furnace trillions of miles away, is a testament to science. The researchers then injected fake planet signals into their treasure trove of data to see what they could detect. They also simulated Earth-mass planets at 2,000 different distances from the primary star, tracking each one over 10 million years. "We calculated the boundaries of the habitable zone around the primary star. Then I tested whether an Earth-mass planet could maintain a stable orbit at different distances within that zone," explains Skylar D'Angiolillo, an Earth and planetary sciences researcher at UCR and one of the study's co-authors. "What we found is that stable orbits are possible in the habitable zone of the primary star. You might expect the second star to disrupt those orbits, but that isn't necessarily what happens." The researchers were also able to rule out the presence of Jupiter-mass-or-larger giant exoplanets around the two stars, going out to about five astronomical units (AU) from the primary star, or about the distance from the Sun at which a Jupiter-mass gas giant exists in our own Solar System (hint: Jupiter ). This is intriguing because in 1855, British astronomer William Jacob claimed that 70 Oph AB had a planet, making it the first host of an exoplanet candidate, University of Michigan (U-M) researchers point out . Jacob's claim didn't survive scrutiny, but more recent measurements showed a 'wobble' that could still have been explained by a Jupiter-sized planet. Instead, this supposed planetary signal appears to have been due to plain old stellar activity, the bane of the RV method. "It's a mix of disappointment and excitement," says Yiting Li, an astronomer at U-M and the study's first author. "We're finding out that there isn't a Jupiter-sized planet, but we're also opening the latest chapter on this historic system." However, terrestrial planets remain below the detection threshold. So, importantly, this suggests that Earth-mass planets could still exist here, as the researchers modeled where they're most likely to be found and to be stable – providing a framework that can be used for other binaries as well. And, according to NASA , "More than half of all stars in the sky have one or more partners," so this can significantly expand our future exploration efforts. Especially when next-(next)-generation observations come online, such as NASA's promising Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), designed to specifically explore and directly image alien worlds. "Overall, our results demonstrate that it is possible for the 70 Oph system to host planets on S-type orbits around the primary star, including terrestrial planets on stable orbits within the [habitable zone] region," the researchers conclude . "If stellar binaries can host Earth-like planets, 70 Oph is one of the best places to look." The research has been published in The Astrophysical Journal . sources.evidenceText: For decades, the amygdala has been cast as the brain's fear center, the almond-shaped structure deep near the brain stem that scientists believed single-handedly orchestrated our responses to danger. Yet a fundamental puzzle has always shadowed that assumption. When a threat first appears, amygdala neurons fire only briefly, a sharp burst of activity that fades almost as quickly as it begins. If the amygdala's alarm is so short-lived, why do defensive behaviors such as freezing, fleeing, or fighting persist for so long afterward? Why does the body remain locked in high-alert mode long after the initial neural spark has died down? A team of neuroscientists at the Salk Institute believes it has found the answer in a tiny, overlooked sliver of brain tissue that has been hiding in plain sight for decades, and their discovery could reshape how researchers think about fear, panic, and the disorders that arise when fear refuses to switch off. The region in question is called the amygdalostriatal transition zone, abbreviated ASt, and it sits at the boundary between the amygdala and the striatum, wedged between the basolateral and central subdivisions of the amygdala. According to the new study, published in the journal Neuron on September 14, 2026, ASt neurons behave in a way that the amygdala's neurons do not: they fire with both greater strength and greater longevity in response to danger cues. Where the amygdala sounds a brief first alarm, the ASt appears to sustain the signal, providing the neural substrate that keeps defensive behaviors running after the initial detection of threat has passed. In other words, the ASt may be the missing piece that explains the temporal gap between the brain's rapid detection of danger and the prolonged behavioral response that follows it. The path to this discovery was far from straightforward. The ASt is a difficult target for neuroscientists. It is tiny, it is hard to reach with recording and manipulation tools, and it is hard to distinguish anatomically from the larger, better-studied regions that surround it. Because of these technical challenges, the area had been largely ignored, and researchers were not even certain whether it qualified as a distinct brain region at all. Many simply treated it as an unremarkable transition between the amygdala and the striatum, a boundary zone with no special identity or function of its own. The Salk team's first landmark achievement was to demonstrate that the mouse ASt is in fact a distinct brain region, separate from both the neighboring amygdala and the striatum, with its own definable boundaries and characteristics. Co-corresponding author Kay Tye, a professor at Salk and holder of the Wylie Vale Chair, as well as a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator, described how the field's long-standing focus on the amygdala had blinded researchers to what lay between its subdivisions. People always thought the amygdala was the fear center while ignoring the space between the basolateral and central amygdala entirely, she noted. In the amygdala, firing occurs right at the beginning of the danger, but that raised the question of what happens afterward, what causes the lingering fear, and whether the amygdalostriatal transition zone might be responsible. Her lab's work suggests that the answer to that question is yes, and that the sustained firing properties of ASt neurons are precisely what bridge the gap between brief detection and prolonged defense. Co-corresponding author Fergil Mills, a former postdoctoral researcher in Tye's lab who is now an assistant professor at the University of Utah, emphasized the region's strategic position in the brain's architecture. The ASt sits at a crossroads between the brain's systems for emotional associations and action selection, he explained, yet its function had remained largely unknown until now. That anatomical position is significant. Emotional associations, encoded in circuits like the amygdala, tell an animal what to fear, while action selection systems, including the striatum, determine what the animal does about it. A region positioned between the two, capable of sustained activity, is ideally placed to translate a fleeting emotional signal into a persistent behavioral program such as freezing or avoidance. To characterize the ASt's role in the danger response, the researchers combined electrophysiology with calcium imaging, two complementary techniques for monitoring neural activity. Electrophysiology records the electrical impulses of individual neurons with millisecond precision, while calcium imaging tracks activity across populations of cells over longer periods. Together, these methods revealed that ASt neurons mount a robust and sustained response to danger cues, in marked contrast to the brief firing pattern observed in the amygdala. This sustained activity profile provides a mechanistic explanation for why defensive behaviors like freezing can persist long after the initial threat signal has been detected, resolving a question that the amygdala-centric view of fear could not answer. The team then went beyond observation to test causation, using targeted stimulation and inhibition of ASt neurons in a mouse model. When the researchers stimulated the ASt, the animals exhibited freezing and avoidance behaviors, the classic defensive responses to perceived danger. When they inhibited the region, the experiments revealed something more specific: a particular subset of dopamine-expressing neurons within the ASt is necessary for the animal to mount fear responses at all. The involvement of dopamine in this context is notable, since the neurotransmitter is more commonly associated with reward and motivation, and its role in a sustained fear circuit underscores how intertwined the brain's emotional and motivational systems really are. sources.evidenceText: NEW YORK - Today, the Trump administration announced sanctions on the entire International Criminal Court, only hours after one of the court’s former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize. Previously, the United States had sanctioned specific ICC officials, a UN human rights expert, and three Palestinian human rights groups. The international community, including the United States, established the ICC in 1998 to help maintain international peace and security. The ICC investigates and prosecutes atrocity crimes when domestic legal systems are unwilling or unable to do so. 125 countries have joined the international treaty creating the ICC, known as the “Rome Statute.” While the United States has not ratified the Rome Statute, it has supported the ICC’s critical work on a wide range of matters under both Democratic and Republican administrations. “The Trump administration's continued attempts to dismantle the International Criminal Court are disastrous for global justice and human rights accountability,” said Jamil Dakwar, director of the ACLU's Human Rights Program. “We condemn the latest sanctions, which could undercut the ICC's ability to investigate and prosecute atrocities such as genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes, and make it even harder for survivors to get justice. We cannot move backwards and let the Trump administration take the world further down a path of impunity and injustice." The ACLU represents two U.S. human rights advocates in a federal lawsuit challenging President Trump’s initial sanctions targeting the ICC on Feb. 6, 2025. As the lawsuit explains, the sanctions violate the First Amendment by prohibiting the advocates, and other Americans like them, from communicating with the ICC, including by providing legal advice, expert analysis, and evidence. In August, the ACLU and 10 other civil liberties and human rights organizations belonging to the International Network of Civil Liberties Organizations (INCLO) called on the European Commission to protect individuals and organizations targeted by U.S. ICC sanctions from their extra-territorial reach by immediately activating the Council of Europe Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 (‘the Blocking Statute’).

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said. The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away." The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said. AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva. Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it." AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training. It could allow researchers to investigate prehistoric populations in sites where conventional archaeological evidence is absent or excavation is restricted to protect fragile rock art. The research began with the hypothesis that Palaeolithic artists might have mixed pigments with saliva before blowing them on to cave walls to create paintings. If saliva became trapped on the rock surface, the researchers reasoned, some of the artists’ DNA might have survived. The team subsequently expanded its investigation to other caves, eventually finding evidence that supported the hypothesis that human DNA could persist on ancient rock surfaces. Between 2022 and 2025, the researchers collected samples from 11 caves across Spain and Portugal. More unexpectedly, the researchers also detected ancient human DNA on several unpainted sections of cave walls at Escoural and Covarón, in Asturias, northern Spain. The findings suggest that genetic material can remain on rock long after direct human contact, whether through touching the surface, leaning against it or handling pigments during the production of paintings. The presence of DNA on unpainted surfaces indicates that the potential of cave walls as genetic archives extends beyond areas containing visible artistic remains. The study brought together researchers from the University of Extremadura, the regional government of Extremadura and the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, a leading centre for ancient DNA research. The Spanish institutions helped initiate the investigation to learn more about the people responsible for the rock paintings at Maltravieso, a site situated within the urban area of Cáceres. The First Art project was promoted by archaeologists Hipólito Collado and José Julio García Arranz, both members of the Patrimonio&ARTE group, which specialises in the conservation and investigation of artistic heritage. García Arranz described the findings as a significant advance for archaeology because they introduce a source of genetic evidence that does not depend on recovering human remains. “Until now, genetic information about prehistoric populations came mainly from skeletal remains, archaeological sediments or tools made from organic materials,” he said. “The possibility of recovering DNA directly from walls allows us to incorporate a completely new source of information to reconstruct human presence and behaviour in the past.” The method could be particularly useful in caves where no human remains have been discovered or where excavation is impossible because of the need to preserve archaeological deposits and rock art. According to García Arranz, the technique offers a way to obtain genetic information without disturbing archaeological layers or putting paintings at risk. Its application could therefore extend investigations into sites that have remained difficult to study through conventional archaeological methods. sources.evidenceText: Intensive breathing exercises can reduce blood flow to the brain by up to 45% and alter communication between brain networks, according to a new brain-imaging study. Participants reported experiences resembling some effects of psychedelic drugs, including altered perception, vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity and changes in self-experience. The researchers, presenting the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich, say changes in brain communication, rather than reduced blood flow alone, appear to be key to the altered state. The study involved 30 healthy, experienced breathwork practitioners who performed high-ventilation breathwork during MRI scanning. Participants reported strong altered states of consciousness, describing a predominantly oceanic state – in other words, a deep feeling of connection to the universe - resembling that of a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin, albeit with less pronounced visual effects. Brain imaging showed that global grey-matter cerebral blood flow fell by around 45% during the session, on average from 16.24 to 9.81 ml/100g/min. Those who reported stronger altered states also showed greater changes in the brain's default mode network, which is involved in self-reflection and self-related thinking. The researchers suggest that the intensity of the experience is not simply explained by reduced blood flow. Instead, the experience might track more closely with changes in communication within the default mode network, a brain system linked to self-reflection and self-related thought. Lead researcher Dr Christian Schmitz, Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim in Germany, said: " Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood. Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate". 'Co-Coordinator, Hana Adolphi said, " Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness. Understanding these mechanisms could also help inform future research into novel approaches for mental health treatment. Nevertheless, this was a relatively small study, and the findings should be considered preliminary. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these brain changes have clinical relevance." Commenting, Dr Guy Fincham (Brighton and Sussex Medical School, UK) said: "This study is intriguing as it is starting to extend findings from recent breathwork research that intensive breathing practices may yield altered states of consciousness which individuals describe in ways analogous to psychedelic compounds, and under brain-imaging conditions. These findings are important because such altered subjective experiences may be harnessed for the improvement of mental health, and an accessible non-pharmacological route such a breathwork could prove invaluable for many. We should note that the study was uncontrolled and the sample was made up of experienced practitioners, so replication of this in breathwork-naïve participants using a randomised-controlled design will help determine whether these findings can translate more widely and produce therapeutic benefit". Dr Fincham was not involved in this study; this is an independent comment. Professor David Nutt (of Imperial College, London) said: "Breathwork is a non-pharmacological bridge to our research into psychedelics, so research which helps us understand how it functions is welcome". Professor Nutt was not involved in this study; this is an independent comment. Antarctica is generally associated with extreme cold, immense ice sheets and one of the most inhospitable environments on Earth. Yet beneath that frozen landscape lies evidence of an entirely different geological past, one that may have helped shape the development of complex life across the planet. New research by geologists Bei Chen and Ian H. Campbell of the Australian National University suggests that Antarctica was once dominated by enormous mountain systems formed during the assembly of Gondwana, the ancient southern supercontinent. Their findings, published in Earth and Planetary Science Letters , indicate that these mountains were part of one of the most significant episodes of mountain building in Earth's geological history. More importantly, the researchers propose that the erosion of those mountains supplied enormous quantities of nutrients to ancient oceans, helping support biological productivity and changes in atmospheric oxygen. Those changes may have contributed to the conditions surrounding the Cambrian explosion, a period when animal life underwent extraordinary diversification. The study does not establish that Antarctica alone caused this transformation. It provides new geological evidence supporting a wider explanation of how continental movements, erosion, ocean chemistry and biological evolution may have been connected. Hundreds of millions of years ago, the continents occupied very different positions from those familiar today. Antarctica, Australia, Africa, South America and the Indian subcontinent formed major parts of Gondwana, a vast southern landmass assembled through a series of continental collisions. These collisions generated enormous geological pressures. As sections of Earth's crust were compressed, rocks were uplifted into mountain systems potentially comparable in scale to the modern Himalayas. Scientists have long suspected that Gondwana's formation produced exceptionally large mountain ranges, but reconstructing their original extent has proved difficult. Over hundreds of millions of years, erosion removed much of the exposed rock. Subsequent continental movement and Antarctica's expanding ice cover further concealed the geological evidence. The new research offers another means of reconstructing this lost landscape. Rather than physically uncovering the ancient mountains, scientists examined microscopic mineral grains that preserve evidence of their geological origins. Central to the discovery are zircons, durable minerals that can survive weathering, erosion, transport and burial over extraordinary periods of geological time. Zircons contain small quantities of uranium, which decays into lead at predictable rates. By measuring these elements, geologists can determine when the minerals crystallised and identify characteristics of the geological environments in which they formed. Chen and Campbell examined zircon grains recovered from sediments associated with Antarctica and compared their characteristics with a wider global geological database. The evidence revealed a particularly important period of mountain-building activity between approximately 650 million and 450 million years ago. This interval coincides with the assembly of Gondwana and overlaps the broader period during which complex animal life became increasingly abundant and diverse. A related September 2026 study, also involving Chen and Campbell, found that much of Antarctica's preserved geological record reflects this relatively late period of continental development. Together, the studies suggest that Antarctica was a major centre of geological activity during Gondwana's formation rather than simply an ancient, stable block of continental crust. One of the most striking findings concerns Antarctica's contribution to the global geological record. According to the researchers, approximately 46 percent of detrital zircons in their weighted global database for the period from the beginning of the Cambrian to the end of the Cambrian explosion were attributed to Antarctic sources. They also estimated that 55 percent of the high-pressure zircon grains in that dataset originated from Antarctica. These figures are significant because they suggest that geological processes associated with Antarctica were exceptionally prominent during this period. The percentages refer to the researchers' weighted zircon database, not to 46 percent of all minerals on Earth or a direct measurement of Antarctica's share of global erosion. The results depend on geological sampling, mineral preservation and the methods used to reconstruct the origins of ancient sediments. Nevertheless, the scale of the Antarctic contribution strengthens the argument that Gondwana's mountain systems were among the dominant geological features of their time. The proposed connection between ancient mountains and the rise of complex life involves a series of linked physical and biological processes. When large mountain ranges form, their exposed rocks become subject to weathering and erosion. Rainfall, rivers and other natural processes break down these rocks, transporting sediments and dissolved minerals into surrounding environments. Among the materials released are nutrients that can influence biological productivity in the oceans. El-Obeid, once home to around 500,000 residents, has become a critical refuge for people displaced by Sudan's civil war, with unofficial estimates placing its current population at nearly 3 million. The city has emerged as a strategic humanitarian and commercial hub linking central Sudan with Darfur, making its stability vital for aid operations across the region. The warning comes days after the UN Human Rights Council approved an urgent investigation into alleged violations and abuses in and around El-Obeid, citing an imminent risk of mass atrocities as violence continues to escalate. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has described the situation as a "red alert," warning that the city could face another humanitarian catastrophe if fighting continues unchecked. For weeks, El-Obeid has been subjected to repeated drone attacks, with strikes damaging power stations, fuel depots, water infrastructure, schools, health facilities, markets, and other civilian sites. The attacks have disrupted electricity and essential services while killing and injuring dozens of civilians. According to UNICEF, at least 330 children were killed or injured across Sudan during the first six months of 2026, with Darfur and Kordofan recording the highest number of child casualties. Since May alone, North Kordofan has witnessed more than 35 child casualties, many resulting from drone strikes, which accounted for around 60% of reported child casualties in the state. Humanitarian organizations have also reported worsening displacement around El-Obeid. Save the Children said more than 5,500 children have been displaced from the city and surrounding areas in just the past two weeks as insecurity and shortages of food, fuel, and clean water continue to deepen. The broader conflict shows no signs of easing. Fighting has intensified across Sudan's three Kordofan states—North, South, and West—where clashes between the SAF and RSF have expanded since late last year. The region has become one of the war's principal battlegrounds, with civilians increasingly trapped between frontlines and humanitarian access severely restricted. International concern has also grown following a recent UN fact-finding mission that concluded the RSF committed acts amounting to genocide during its 2025 campaign in Darfur. UN investigators have warned that similar patterns of violence could emerge in El-Obeid if urgent international action is not taken to protect civilians and secure humanitarian access. Sudan has been engulfed in civil war since April 2023, when fighting erupted between the Sudanese army and the RSF over disagreements concerning the integration of the paramilitary force into the national military. The conflict has since killed tens of thousands of people, displaced approximately 13 million, and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises, with more than 30 million people now in need of humanitarian assistance.
